sections.overview: The Chinese sparrowhawk is a small migratory raptor that breeds in East Asia and winters in Southeast Asia and the Indonesian region. Its migration can involve long sea crossings and large seasonal movements through places such as Korea and Taiwan. In its breeding range it is particularly associated with wooded landscapes near wetlands and rice fields, where frogs are an important prey.
sections.identification: Adults have a compact body, a broad head and relatively short, rounded wings. The male is blue-grey above, with a rusty wash on the breast, pale underparts and dark red eyes; the female is similar but larger, with yellower eyes and stronger warm-brown tones on the breast. Both sexes show conspicuous black tips to the flight feathers, an especially useful mark in flight. Juveniles are brown above and streaked below. Published measurements give a total length of about 25–35 cm and wingspan of 52–62 cm; males weigh about 106–140 g and females 125–204 g. The female is therefore appreciably larger and heavier. No meaningful height or body-width figure was located. The broad head, compact shape and dark primary tips help separate it from other migrating accipiters; age and sex alter the underside pattern.
sections.habitat: It breeds in lowland and foothill woodland, often near wetlands, streams and rice paddies, and uses open ground to forage. It migrates south through East and Southeast Asia to wintering areas including the Philippines, Indonesia and nearby islands. Satellite tracking of birds from southern China documented long-distance migration with stopovers near forest and water; those tracks represent a small sample rather than the entire population.
sections.diet: It takes frogs, small birds and insects, with the balance changing between seasons and regions. In a Korean breeding study, frogs made up about 65–75% of prey delivered to chicks in two nest groups; the Korean National Institute of Ecology also notes cicadas and occasional small birds in chick diet. This frog-rich diet explains its association with paddy fields and other wetlands during breeding, but should not be assumed for every wintering site.
sections.behavior: During migration it may gather in visible flocks and use thermals to gain height before crossing water. On breeding grounds it hunts near woodland edges and open wet fields. A long-term study of eight pairs in Korea recorded small home ranges and territorial defense around nests; the results describe one study area and season, not a universal territory size.
sections.reproduction: Pairs nest in trees, often in wooded habitat beside fields or wetlands. A Korean field study found a mean clutch of 4.1 eggs, an average incubation period of about 19.5 days and a nestling period of about 19.4 days in the nests followed. A more recent regional account reports three to four eggs and a longer incubation estimate, showing that study method and local conditions matter. The male and female both attend the nest, though the female spends more time incubating and brooding.
sections.ecology: As a predator of frogs, insects and small birds, it links wet agricultural fields and adjacent woodland. It can be especially dependent on amphibian prey during breeding, so loss of wetlands, reduced rice-field habitat and pesticide-related declines in frogs may affect local breeding success. Migratory populations also depend on suitable stopover habitat across multiple countries.
sections.conservation: The species is assessed as Least Concern globally, but it is legally protected and considered threatened in South Korea, where breeding numbers have declined. This difference reflects regional rather than global status. Wetland and woodland protection, safer pesticide use and maintaining migration stopovers are relevant conservation measures; global LC status should not obscure local declines.
